sec.title: Background
sec.p: In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we aimed to explore the availability of alternatives to oxytocin for preventing postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) during vaginal births (VB) and caesarean births (CB).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We followed the Cochrane guidelines for the review, and reported the results using the PRISMA guidelines. Using a thorough search strategy, we retrieved original articles from SCOPUS, PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library from January 2015 to February 2025. We analyzed the RCTs to compare Tranexamic Acid (TXA), carbetocin, and misoprostol with oxytocin for preventing PPH in both vaginal and caesarean births. The review's protocol has been officially registered with PROSPERO under the identifier CRD420251002602.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A meta-analysis of 20 trials showed no statistically significant difference in reducing blood loss during vaginal births (SMD = − 0.21; 95% CI − 0.62 to 0.19; I2 = 96%). However, contrasting results were observed in cesarean births (SMD = − 0.82; 95% CI − 1.49 to − 0.16; p = 0.02). Correspondingly, no statistically significant difference was found in the occurrence of PPH in vaginal births (OR = 0.80; 95% CI 0.53 to 1.21; I2 = 98%), while significant variances were detected in cesarean births (OR = 0.58; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.80; I2 = 21%). Hemoglobin variation was notably lower in both vaginal and cesarean births (SMD = − 0.32; 95% CI − 0.49 to − 0.16; I2 = 93%) and (SMD = − 0.90; 95% CI − 1.52 to − 0.27; I2 = 96%), respectively.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Considering the substantial heterogeneity and mostly non-significant pooled results, the current findings should be viewed as indicative rather than conclusive. Further rigorous, well-designed randomized controlled trials are necessary to better define their effectiveness, optimize dosing, and identify patient groups most likely to benefit.
Keywords: Postpartum hemorrhage, Oxytocin, Carbetocin, Tranexamic acid, Misoprostol, Vaginal birth, Cesarean birth, PPH prevention, Low-resource settings

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is one of the most serious complications observed during the postnatal period. It is characterized as a loss of blood of greater than 500 ml during vaginal births (VB) and 1000 mL with caesarean births (CB) [1]. According to a World Health Organization statement (2023), over fourteen million postnatal mothers experience PPH, leading to 70,000 deaths among postnatal mothers [2]. According to the 2020 report, the global maternal mortality rate (MMR) is 223 per 100,000 live births. Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3.1 states that by 2030, the MMR should be less than 70 per 100,000 live births. Despite continued international efforts, women's mortality rates have lately slowed, emphasizing the critical need for new treatments to prevent and cure PPH [2].

PPH is mainly caused by uterine atony, which results in a prolonged 3rd stage of labor in 70 to 80% of cases. Primary PPH risk factors include the retention of placental or fetal products, advanced maternal age, previous PPH, uterine rupture, hypertensive diseases in pregnancy, and bleeding disorders such as placenta previa and placental abruption [3–5]. PPH prevention requires strategic planning, early diagnosis of high-risk mothers, and a treatment approach that targets the underlying causes and severity of the condition [1].

Oxytocin is the first-line uterotonic for PPH prevention and management according to WHO guidelines, and because of its demonstrated efficacy, hospitals frequently use it. However, because of its short half-life (3–5 min), need for continuous administration, cold-chain storage requirements (2–8 °C), and requirement for qualified healthcare providers for intravenous or intramuscular injection, its availability in community health settings is questionable [5]. Demand is rising due to the growing number of PPH patients, highlighting the need for easily accessible substitutes [1, 6, 7]. These issues increase the need for inexpensive, heat-stable, and simple-to-administer solutions, especially in places where access to emergency obstetric care is scarce [3].

Other uterotonics, including misoprostol, carbetocin, and tranexamic acid (TXA), are being investigated as preventive therapy for PPH management and its prevention in VB and CB due to these difficulties. Lower dosages are required for the long-acting uterotonic carbetocin. Notably, heat-stable carbetocin (HSC) is perfect for low-resource healthcare settings because it doesn't need to be refrigerated. In circumstances where oxytocin maintenance cannot be guaranteed, WHO included HSC in its 2018 PPH prevention guidelines [8]. Studies show that HSC can be kept at 30 °C for at least three years without refrigeration and is just as effective as oxytocin at reducing PPH [9, 10]. The potential of TXA, an antifibrinolytic drug, to reduce and prevent PPH during and after delivery has been thoroughly investigated [11]. TXA is an effective medication for PPH prevention and treatment, especially in anemic women, according to the WOMAN-2 Trial (2024). Early TXA treatment lowers the risk of severe bleeding and hemodynamic instability by dramatically reducing postpartum blood loss. Additionally, it lessens the need for blood transfusions, which is especially helpful in environments with limited resources. IV is an appealing substitute for oxytocin because it effectively delivers TXA and doesn't need to be refrigerated, especially in rural and community healthcare settings [12]. Furthermore, the trials support the safety of TXA by demonstrating no appreciable rise in thromboembolic events. Its demonstrated effectiveness, safety profile, and ease of administration support its usage in traditional PPH prevention and care, providing a cost-effective and convenient way to lower maternal morbidity and mortality. [13].

Misoprostol, a prostaglandin E1 analog, is a potent uterotonic medication because it can be administered orally, sublingually, or rectally and is stable in hot temperatures. Because misoprostol does not require refrigeration, unlike oxytocin, it can be used in home deliveries and community health infrastructure. Misoprostol is commonly used for PPH prophylaxis; however, because of its side effects, including fever, chills, and gastrointestinal distress, careful dosage modification is required to ensure both safety and efficacy [14].
Given the practical challenges of administering oxytocin in community healthcare facilities, this review aims to:

list-item.p: Investigate the efficacy of carbetocin, tranexamic acid, and misoprostol in reducing PPH among mothers undergoing vaginal births and caesarean births.
Explore the availability and potential of alternatives to oxytocin for preventing PPH during VB and CB.

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: In this review, the PRISMA standards [15] were followed, and the systematic review and meta-analysis were carried out using the procedures given in the Cochrane Handbook [16]. The review protocol was officially registered with PROSPERO under the identifier CRD420251002602 for the year 2025.

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: We thoroughly assessed digital medical archives, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library, evaluating data from 1 January 2015, to February 2025. Based on the PICO (population, intervention, control, and outcome) framework, a search was conducted using key terms, and two authors independently searched the databases for randomized controlled studies. Our digital searching procedure was developed and evaluated using the Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies (PRESS) checklist as a validation tool [17]. PPH, postpartum bleeding, oxytocin, carbetocin, misoprostol, caesarean births, and vaginal births are key terms to search for relevant articles in the included databases (Tables 1).

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: Population: Women at term gestation, without PPH, who had undergone vaginal and caesarean births.
Intervention: Administration of Carbetocin, Misoprostol, and Tranexamic Acid.
Comparator: Oxytocin only.

Outcomes: The primary outcomes assessed were total blood loss, occurrence of PPH, and variations in Hb levels within 24 h. Secondary outcomes included variations in blood transfusion requirements. Additional factors considered were uterotonic agents, invasive non-surgical interventions, and surgical procedures.
Study Design: Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were considered.

Studies were omitted if they were reviews, non-RCTs, conference abstracts, case reports, case series, or RCTs conducted without oxytocin as the control group. Furthermore, non-English publications and studies assessing unrelated outcomes were excluded.

sec.title: Study selection process
sec.p: Relevant RCTs were identified through a two-stage screening process by searching four databases. The process began with a review of titles and abstracts, after which the articles that satisfied the initial criteria underwent detailed full-text assessment. These articles were assessed for the robustness of their evidence for meta-analysis and their overall suitability for this review. Three reviewers conducted the screening independently, with any disputes determined by a 3rd reviewer.

sec.title: Data extraction process
sec.p: Two reviewers using a preformatted online extraction tool independently collected data. The following information was collected: (1) research design, (2) study population features, (3) assessment of risk bias, and (4) the study outcome comprising total blood loss, PPH occurrence, and Hb variations within 24 h, blood transfusion requirements, additional usage of uterotonic agents, invasive non-surgical interventions, and surgical procedures. Any differences were addressed and resolved through conversations moderated by the 3rd author.

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: The two reviewers separately examined the quality of the papers incorporated using the ROB-II approach (Figs. 2 and 3) for the included article [18]. The Cochrane risk of bias framework was applied, covering domains such as generating randomization sequences, securing apportionment concealment, participant and researcher blinding, masking of outcome evaluation, management of missing outcome data, bias in selective reporting, and other possible risk factors for bias. Each RCT was evaluated for low, high, or uncertain risk of bias, and a 3rd author resolved any discrepancies between assessors.

sec.title: Data synthesis
sec.p: For dichotomous data, we used odds ratios to merge the total events with the total samples of the intervention and oxytocin groups. In the current review, the population was heterogeneous, so we applied the inverse variance technique using a random-effects model. For continuous data, we calculated the mean difference (MD) among the groups from the initial assessment to the final evaluation, incorporating the standard deviation (SD) and sample size per group for each efficacy outcome, using a similar approach. To assess study heterogeneity, forest plots were inspected and the I2 statistic was used in the most recent RevMan Web version (available at https://revman.cochrane.org/myReviews). In this review, potential publication bias in the included studies was assessed using funnel plots [19].

sec.title: Analysis of subgroups
sec.p: Analysis of subgroups was conducted considering the amount of blood loss, the requirement for blood transfusion, PPH occurrence, and additional uterotonic agent usage, specifically comparing carbetocin and oxytocin, misoprostol and oxytocin, and TXA and Oxytocin in VB and CB. SMDs with 95% CIs were calculated using a random-effects model. The Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman (HKSJ) adjustment was used to conduct the subgroup analysis, and between-study heterogeneity was estimated using the DerSimonian–Laird (DL) method for τ2. Heterogeneity is expressed as I2. The diamond indicates the overall pooled outcome for each subgroup. A P-value below 0.05 was deemed statistically significant, indicating adequate evidence to refute the null hypothesis. Heterogeneity was assessed using a P-value threshold of < 0.1 and an I2 value beyond 50%, indicative of substantial heterogeneity.

sec.title: Sensitivity analysis
sec.p: To make sure that no single article unduly affected the overall effect size, we used a leave-one-out strategy, removing each study in turn. Additionally, we assessed the quality of the studies and classified them as great RoB, low RoB, or some concerns.

sec.title: Characteristics of included studies
sec.p: Of the 1140 distinct documents retrieved in the initial search, 666 were removed as they were duplicates. After the title and abstract screening, 280 more documents were removed. After the full-text screening of the 194 documents, 20 documents were included in this analysis, eight of which were on cesarean delivery and twelve of which were on vaginal delivery. The data on the characteristics of vaginal and cesarean deliveries are shown in Tables 1 and 2 [20–39]. We manually examined the bibliographies of the selected research papers but did not identify any additional studies for consideration. sec.title: Assessment of quality of studies
sec.p: Figures 2 and 3 show that, based on the RoB evaluation, the complete classification of studies reveals that seven exhibit a low RoB. In comparison, 10 studies indicate some concerns; four are categorized as possessing a high RoB. The primary areas of concern lie in the randomization process (D1) and missing outcome data (D3), where three studies have a high RoB due to randomization issues, and five studies face a high risk due to missing data. Among all the bias domains assessed, deviations from intended interventions (D2) and measurement of outcomes (D4) appear to be the least problematic, with D4 demonstrating an overwhelmingly low risk, as 20 studies fall into this category. Similarly, D5 presents minimal concerns, with only three studies classified as high risk.

sec.title: Publication bias
sec.p: Figures 4, 5, 6, and 7 present funnel plots showing the distribution of studies around the pooled effect estimate (vertical dashed line at SMD ≈ 0). Most data points for misoprostol, tranexamic acid, and carbetocin cluster symmetrically near the center, particularly among studies with smaller standard errors in the upper part of the plots. This pattern indicates a low risk of publication bias and good precision among larger studies. Overall, the plots suggest no substantial publication bias and support the stability and reliability of the meta-analysis findings.

sec.title: Postpartum blood loss
sec.p: Ten randomized controlled trials (RCTs) [20–28, 31], including a total of 108,802 participants, evaluated the efficacy of misoprostol, TXA, and carbetocin compared with oxytocin in reducing blood loss in women with vaginal delivery. Employing a random-effects model, the investigation revealed that these uterotonic agents were minimally associated with reduced postpartum bleeding in the intervention group (SMD = − 0.21; 95% CI − 0.62 to 0.19; P = 0.31) compared to the oxytocin group. However, the 95% CI (− 0.62 to 0.19) still crosses zero, with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 96%). No significant differences were observed between subgroups (Fig. 8). The certainty of clinical evidence is low because the pooled effects were not statistically significant and substantial heterogeneity was present across studies and subgroups.

sec.p: Eight RCTs [32–39] including 3537 participants, evaluated the effect of experimental interventions with control group on postpartum blood loss within 24 h of CB. The random-effects meta-analysis revealed a statistically significant reduction in blood loss favoring the experimental interventions compared with oxytocin (SMD = − 0.82; 95% CI − 1.49 to − 0.16; p = 0.02). The overall analysis showed considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 98%; χ2 = 294.58, df = 7, p < 0.00001), this guided us to conduct the subgroup analysis. However, in the subgroup analysis, carbetocin showed a non-significant effect, whereas the TXA subgroup demonstrated a large and statistically significant reduction in blood loss (SMD = − 1.28; 95% CI − 2.09 to − 0.47; p = 0.01). (Fig. 9). Due to high heterogeneity among the included studies, the strength of the evidence is limited, and further high-quality randomized controlled trials are required.

sec.title: Occurrence of PPH in vaginal and caesarean births
Occurrence of PPH in vaginal births
sec.p: The occurrence of PPH was 21,230 out of 49,497 (42.28%) in the experimental group and 15,843 out of 49,249 (32.2%) in the control group, where mothers received oxytocin. The interventional group included women who received carbetocin [20–22, 26, 31], TXA [24, 27, 28], and misoprostol [23, 25, 30]. The pooled analysis demonstrated no statistically significant difference between the experimental and control groups (OR = 0.80; 95% CI 0.53–1.21; p = 0.26), with very high heterogeneity (I2 = 98%). There was no significant difference between subgroups (p = 0.31), indicating comparable effects across interventions. (Fig. 10). Due to high heterogeneity among the included studies and non-significant pooled effects, the strength of the evidence is limited, and further high-quality randomized controlled trials are required.

sec.title: Occurrence of PPH in caesarean births
sec.p: The occurrence of PPH was 4.16% (72/1729) among women who received Carbetocin [35–37] and TXA [32–34, 38, 39], and 6.91% (125/1808) among those who received oxytocin. With an odds ratio of 0.58 (95% CI 0.43–0.80, p = 0.0008), this indicates a 42% reduction in the occurrence of PPH in the Carbetocin and TXA group. Low heterogeneity among the studies included in this analysis is indicated by the I2 value of 21%. According to the subgroup analysis, there was no significant difference in the carbetocin group; however, the TXA group showed a significant reduction in the occurrence of PPH (OR = 0.44, 95% CI 0.28–0.68; p = 0.0002), with minimal heterogeneity (I2 = 9%), demonstrating the robustness of this finding (Fig. 11).

sec.title: Hemoglobin variations within 24 h following vaginal and caesarean births
Hemoglobin variations within 24 h following vaginal births
sec.p: Nine RCTs [22–28, 30, 31], which included 34,201 participants, assessed how misoprostol, TXA, and carbetocin affected hemoglobin levels in women giving birth vaginally comparing with oxytocin. The overall pooled analysis demonstrates a statistically significant reduction in the outcome in the experimental group compared with control (SMD = − 0.32, 95% CI − 0.49 to − 0.16; p = 0.002) with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 93%) due to the variability among the included studies. However, in the subgroup analysis, tranexamic acid and misoprostol did not show statistically significant effects, whereas carbetocin showed a statistically significant effect; however, heterogeneity was considerably high across all three subgroup analyses. It is indicating that there is no clear evidence that the effect differs between the intervention (Fig. 12).

sec.title: Hemoglobin variations within 24 h following caesarean births
sec.p: Eight RCTs [32–39], including 3537 participants, evaluated the effect of carbetocin and TXA on variations in Hb levels among women who underwent caesarean births. The findings revealed that these uterotonic agents were associated with a significant variation in Hb levels (SMD = − 0.90; 95% CI − 1.52 to − 0.27; p = 0.01) (Fig. 13). The heterogeneity (I2 = 96%) is considerably high indicating considerable viability in the included studies, which led us to perform the subgroup analysis. In the subgroup analysis, TXA showed a statistically significant reduction in the outcome, whereas carbetocin did not. These findings are better viewed as supportive or suggestive evidence rather than definitive evidence, and they highlight the need for careful subgroup interpretation and further high-quality, well-standardized studies to confirm the results.

sec.p: The use of additional uterotonics was observed in 151/1697 cases (8.89%) in the experimental group and 251 out of 1840 cases (13.64%) in the control group. The experimental group received Tranexamic acid [32–34, 38, 39] and carbetocin [35–37] individually, while the control group was administered oxytocin. When comparing the experimental groups to the controls, the meta-analysis found no statistically significant decrease in the need for additional uterotonics (OR = 0.40, 95% CI [0.15 to 1.10]; p = 0.07). All of the studies showed significant heterogeneity (I2 = 82%), which reflects the differences in effects between trials (Fig. 15). The subgroup analysis also showed that there was no statistically significant difference between TXA and carbetocin (P for subgroup differences = 0.11). Given the substantial heterogeneity and imprecision of effect estimates, the evidence is insufficient to support a definitive clinical recommendation.

sec.title: Requirement of blood transfusion in VB and CB
Requirement of blood transfusion in VB
sec.p: In the experimental group, 1494 out of 47,105 cases (3.17%) and in the control group, 1806 out of 61,697 cases (2.93%) required blood transfusions because of severe postpartum bleeding. The pooled analysis across all interventions showed no statistically significant difference between experimental and control groups (OR = 1.12, 95% CI [0.74 to 1.68]; p = 0.56). However, the odds ratio reveals a slight increase in the probability of blood transfusion requirement in the experimental group; the CI includes 1.0, indicating that the difference is not statistically significant. The I2 value of 65% reflects moderate heterogeneity among the included studies, which led us to perform subgroup analysis. (Fig. 16). Given the substantial heterogeneity and imprecision of the effect estimates, the current evidence is insufficient to support a definitive clinical recommendation.

sec.title: Requirement of blood transfusion in CB
sec.p: The requirement of blood transfusion due to heavy postpartum bleeding was reported in 18 out of 1769 cases (1.02%) in the experimental group and 37 out of 1,808 cases (2.05%) in the control group. The analysis of randomized studies indicates a statistically non-significant reduction in the need for blood transfusions in the experimental group compared to the control group (OR = 0.44, 95% CI [0.16 to 1.24]; p = 0.10). The I2 value of 43% reflects moderate heterogeneity among the included studies. (Fig. 17). The certainty of evidence is low due to the lack of statistically significant pooled effects, imprecision of estimates, and moderate heterogeneity across studies.

sec.p: The use of surgical interventions among vaginal births was reported in 35 out of 16,027 cases (0.22%) in the experimental group and 47 out of 16,024 women (0.29%) in the control group. In caesarean births, 25 out of 857 cases (2.92%) in the experimental group and 50 out of 889 cases (5.63%) in the control group required invasive, non-surgical intervention. The odds ratio for vaginal births was OR = 0.62 (95% CI [0.11 to 3.65]; I2 = 66%), indicating a non-significant reduction in surgical interventions in the experimental group, with moderate heterogeneity (Fig. 20). For caesarean births, the odds ratio was OR = 0.41 (95% CI [0.10 to 1.64]; I2 = 51%), also indicating a non-significant reduction in surgical interventions, with moderate heterogeneity across the studies (Fig. 21). The evidence indicates no statistically significant reduction in the use of invasive non-surgical or surgical interventions among either vaginal or caesarean births in the experimental group compared with the control group. Due to moderate to substantial heterogeneity across studies, resulting in low certainty of evidence.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (12 vaginal births and 8 cesarean births) involving 113,560 postnatal women found mixed results regarding the effect of carbetocin, TXA, and misoprostol during vaginal and cesarean births. In terms of blood loss exceeding 500 ml in vaginal births [20–28, 31] there was no statistically significant variance between TXA, carbetocin, misoprostol, and oxytocin in reducing blood loss (SMD = − 0.21; 95% CI − 0.62 to 0.19; I2 = 96%). However, in the CB, eight RCTs [32–39] including 3537 participants, results suggest a moderate overall effect in favor of the experimental interventions compared with control. The overall analysis showed considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 98%). In the subgroup analysis, carbetocin showed a non-significant effect, whereas the TXA subgroup demonstrated a large and statistically significant reduction in blood loss (SMD = − 1.28; 95% CI − 2.09 to − 0.47; p = 0.01). Due to the high heterogeneity among the included studies, the strength of the evidence is limited. This variability reduces confidence in the pooled estimates and highlights the need for further high-quality randomized controlled trials to provide more robust and reliable evidence.

In terms of the occurrence of PPH events in vaginal births, no statistical Signiant results found between the experimental group (carbetocin, tranexamic acid, and misoprostol) and the control group (oxytocin) in reducing the occurrence of PPH, with an odds ratio (OR = 0.80; 95% CI 0.53–1.21; p = 0.26). In contrast, there was a statistically significant difference in the incidence of PPH between the experimental group (carbetocin and tranexamic acid) and the control group in cesarean deliveries, with an odds ratio (OR = 0.58, 95% CI [0.43 to 0.80]; I2 = 21%). When comparing carbetocin and TXA, carbetocin was not significantly effective in reducing the occurrence of PPH (OR = 0.79, 95% CI [0.50 to 1.23]). In terms of Hb variation, the experimental group was found to be more effective in both vaginal and cesarean births compared to the control group (SMD = − 0.32, 95% CI − 0.49 to − 0.16; p = 0.002) and (SMD = − 0.90; 95% CI − 1.52 to − 0.27; p = 0.01), however, heterogeneity was considerably high across all three subgroup analyses. These findings are better viewed as supportive or suggestive evidence rather than definitive evidence, and they highlight the need for careful subgroup interpretation and further high-quality, well-standardized studies to confirm the results.

The additional use of uterotonics in vaginal births was observed in 9528 out of 32,820 cases (29.03%) in the experimental group and in 13,306 out of 47,480 cases (28.03%) in the control group. No statistically significant difference was found between the experimental and control groups (OR = 0.54, 95% CI [0.26 to 1.13]; I2 = 88%). Similarly, in caesarean births, no significant difference was observed (OR = 0.40, 95% CI [0.15 to 1.10]; p = 0.07). With respect to the need for blood transfusion as a consequence of severe postpartum hemorrhage in vaginal deliveries, there were 1494 of 47,105 (3.17%) in the experimental group and 1806 of 61,697 (2.93%) in the control group who needed transfusion. Although there was a slight increase as suggested by the odds ratio, it was not statistically significant (OR = 1.12, 95% CI [0.74 to 1.68]; I2 = 65%). Similarly, in cesarean section deliveries, there was no significant difference between the two groups regarding transfusion requirements (OR = 0.44, 95% CI [0.16 to 1.24]; I2 = 43%). For both vaginal and cesarean section deliveries, the experimental interventions failed to show a statistically significant advantage over the control group regarding the need for additional uterotonics and blood transfusion. Although there were some differences between the two groups, all the pooled estimates allowed for the possibility of no effect, with considerable heterogeneity, especially in vaginal deliveries. These findings suggest little and inconsistent clinical advantage, and thus, the routine use of these experimental interventions is not currently justified. More carefully designed randomized controlled trials are required to determine their true efficacy.

sec.title: Comparison of TXA with oxytocin in VB and CB
sec.p: Our meta-analysis confirms previous results on the outcome of cesarean delivery. Prophylactic tranexamic acid (TXA) significantly decreased postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), as shown in the Cochrane review by Novikova et al. (nine trials, N = 2453) [40]. Likewise, Li et al. (15 studies, N = 3353) showed that TXA administration resulted in a marked decrease in total blood loss (mean difference [MD] = 154.25 mL) [41]. These results were confirmed by the most recent comprehensive analysis (59 RCTs, N = 18,649) [42]. In the current meta-analysis, cesarean birth (CB) showed a significantly lower rate of PPH reduction after TXA administration than vaginal birth (VB). However, the presence of high heterogeneity among the included studies reduces the strength of the evidence. This heterogeneity reduces confidence in the results and emphasizes the need for further high-quality randomized controlled trials to provide more concrete and reliable results.

The effectiveness of TXA in reducing the incidence of PPH and total blood loss in VB has been confirmed by previous comprehensive reviews and meta-analyses. Preventive TXA administration significantly reduced the incidence of PPH, according to Saccone et al. [43] (four RCTs, n = 4,671). Similarly, Della Corte et al. [44] (two RCTs, n = 14,363) demonstrated that TXA treatment significantly reduced hysterectomy rates. In the current meta-analysis, no significant reduction was found in VB; however, a significant reduction was found in CB, where TXA was more effective than oxytocin. Bellos et al. [45] demonstrated that TXA was associated with a lower risk of total blood loss and beneficial effects on hemoglobin levels; these results are in agreement with our meta-analysis.

sec.title: Comparison of carbetocin with oxytocin in VB and CB
sec.p: In the current meta-analysis, except for hemoglobin variation within 24 h following vaginal and caesarean births, carbetocin did not demonstrate statistically significant effects. No significant reductions were observed in blood loss, incidence of postpartum hemorrhage, requirement for blood transfusion, need for invasive procedures, or use of additional uterotonics when compared with oxytocin in either vaginal or caesarean births. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to non-significant pooled effects and moderate to high heterogeneity. Therefore, this review recommends further high-quality randomized controlled trials to strengthen the evidence. A recent study by Judio J et al. (6 RCTs, n = 3048) demonstrated that carbetocin prophylaxis significantly decreased postpartum hemorrhage in terms of blood loss. The variation in hemoglobin levels before and after delivery, however, was not statistically significant [46]. Maged A et al. (17 studies) also found that using carbetocin significantly lowered the need for blood transfusions, hemoglobin variation (MD = −0.08, 95% CI −0.10 to −0.06), and the use of uterotonic agents (OR = 0.53, 95% CI 0.39–0.72). Furthermore, this study identified no significant variation in the prevalence of PPH [47]. Previous comprehensive evaluations and quantitative syntheses provide strong evidence that carbetocin reduces the occurrence of PPH in vaginal births. Huang et al. (5 RCTs, N = 4,631) reported a substantial decrease in PPH incidence with carbetocin treatment. Additionally, the need for additional uterotonic agents was lower in the carbetocin group compared to the oxytocin group (odds ratio = 0.41, 95% CI [0.29, 0.56], Z = 5.34). However, no significant difference was observed in the proportion of blood transfusions between the carbetocin and oxytocin groups [48]. Similarly, Kalafat et al. (30 studies) reported a considerable reduction in the additional use of uterotonic agents (R = 0.56, 95% CI [0.34–0.94]) and a lower risk of PPH occurrence [49].

sec.title: Comparison of misoprostol with oxytocin in VB and CB
sec.p: In the current meta-analysis, misoprostol did not show statistically significant effects in reducing blood loss, occurrence of postpartum hemorrhage, requirement for blood transfusion, need for additional uterotonics, or requirement for invasive and surgical interventions in either vaginal or caesarean births. However, the strength of these findings is limited due to non-significant pooled effects and high heterogeneity. Tan et al. (6 trials, n = 4,034) reported that women in the misoprostol group had significantly higher rates of PPH and required more additional uterotonic therapy compared with those receiving oxytocin or methylergometrine. However, the misoprostol group required significantly fewer manual removals of the placenta (RR = 0.33, 95% CI 0.15–0.76; P < 0.01) [50]. Conde-Agudelo et al. (13 trials, 3174 women) found notable differences between misoprostol and oxytocin. While rectal misoprostol substantially reduced intraoperative and postpartum blood loss, the combination of sublingual misoprostol plus oxytocin resulted in a significant reduction in mean hematocrit drop (MD = 2.1%; 95% CI − 3.4 to − 0.8) and a lower need for extra uterotonic agents (RR = 0.33, 95% CI 0.18–0.62) compared with oxytocin alone [51]. In low-resource settings, where oxytocin may be unavailable and cold-chain storage cannot be maintained, misoprostol remains an important alternative uterotonic for the prevention and control of PPH [52]. However, misoprostol is associated with several adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, gastrointestinal discomfort, fever, chills, headache, dizziness, and general malaise. Therefore, misoprostol should be used with caution [53, 54].

sec.title: Strengths and limitations
sec.p: To the best of our knowledge, this review is the first to comprehensively compare misoprostol, tranexamic acid (TXA), and carbetocin with oxytocin for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) in both vaginal and cesarean sections. The study pools a massive sample of 113,560 postpartum women from 20 randomized controlled trials, thus improving the power of the study and its generalizability. The study examined a range of clinically important outcomes such as blood loss, incidence of PPH, hemoglobin change, requirement for further uterotonics, and blood transfusion.

Despite the above-stated advantages, there are a number of limitations that deserve mention. The first of these is the high level of heterogeneity that was noted in most of the pooled analyses, especially with regard to outcomes associated with blood loss and hemoglobin change. This is likely due to differences in the study populations, intervention methods, and settings, which greatly reduce the precision of the pooled results. To mitigate this, subgroup analyses were performed, a random-effects model was used in the pooled effect analysis, and funnel plots were employed to investigate publication bias. Furthermore, the number of trials included in some of the subgroup analyses, especially those involving carbetocin and misoprostol, was relatively low.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This meta-analysis provides evidence of the context-dependent and diverse effects of carbetocin, tranexamic acid, and misoprostol in the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage in vaginal and cesarean deliveries. There was no significant benefit observed in vaginal deliveries for blood loss > 500 mL or the incidence of postpartum hemorrhage when comparing the experimental drugs to oxytocin. However, tranexamic acid significantly decreased both blood loss and the incidence of postpartum hemorrhage in cesarean sections, suggesting a more consistent positive effect in this subgroup. Carbetocin and misoprostol did not show a clear superiority over oxytocin for most clinical outcomes in both vaginal and cesarean deliveries, although there was a suggestion of improvement in hemoglobin level changes. The lack of significant reduction in the need for additional uterotonics or blood transfusions further supports the lack of clinical benefit from the routine use of these interventions.

In view of the large heterogeneity and largely non-significant pooled estimates, the current results should be considered suggestive rather than definitive. The routine use of these agents, especially in vaginal deliveries, is not strongly supported by the current evidence. Further rigorous and well-designed randomized controlled trials are required to better define their efficacy, refine their dosing regimens, and identify the subgroups of patients who may most benefit from their use.
